# Security Policy

dsh-minato is an **unofficial**, cross-platform (Windows/Linux) deploy & ops toolkit for DeepSeek Harness (dsh): a CLI, an Avalonia GUI, and an optional read-only bridge plugin.
It handles your dsh data directory (typically `~/.dsh`), files stored inside it, and can
delete data — so treat it as a data-management tool, not just a launcher.

The project is developed in the open ([MIT](LICENSE)); the trust model is **verifiable
mechanisms, not promises**: every release is built from source by GitHub Actions, ships a
CI-generated `hashes.txt` (SHA-256), and the manifest is GPG-signed by the maintainer
(see [Verifiability](#verifiability)).

## Official channels & supply-chain controls

**Official distribution is limited to:**

| Channel | What it provides |
|---|---|
| This GitHub repository | Source of truth (MIT) |
| Its Releases page | The only official binaries (`*.exe`, `*.zip`, `*.tar.gz`) |
| GitHub Actions (this repo's workflows) | The only builder of official binaries |

Third-party mirrors, cloud-drive re-uploads, "paid / cracked / modified" editions and any
other distributor are **not official and not trusted**. The project is free; **no one is
authorized to sell it**.

Controls in force (anti-tampering / anti-poisoning):

- **CI-only builds** — official artifacts are produced by
  [build-release.yml](.github/workflows/build-release.yml) from the tagged commit; there is
  no manual-upload path for official binaries.
- **SHA-256 manifest** — `hashes.txt` is generated by CI from the exact files it built.
- **GPG-signed manifest** — `hashes.txt.asc` (detached signature; the private key lives only
  in GitHub Secrets, never in the repository).
- **Build provenance attestation (an independent extra control)** — tag builds publish GitHub
  artifact attestations; verify with
  `gh attestation verify <file> --repo sakanamaru/dsh-minato`. This is a
  **separate** check layered on top of `verify.ps1`: `verify.ps1` does **not** verify
  attestations, and the attestation does **not** replace the GPG signature check. Neither
  covers the other — see [What the built-in integrity checks prove](#what-the-built-in-integrity-checks-prove-and-do-not-prove).
- **Immutable releases** — enabled 2026-09-14: once a release is published, its metadata and
  assets can no longer be modified or replaced (historical releases included).
- **Tag protection ruleset** — `v*` tags cannot be deleted or moved (`deletion` +
  `non_fast_forward`, bypass: never).
- **Least-privilege CI** — per-job `permissions:` (test job read-only); third-party actions
  pinned to commit SHAs.
- **Draft-then-publish release flow** — a release is created as a **draft**, the tag build
  attaches assets once, then it is published; post-publish changes are impossible by design.
  (Consequence: release notes/assets must be final before publishing; corrections go into a
  new release.)

Verify any download before running it — see [Verifiability](#verifiability) and the
"Official distribution" section of the README.

## Update channel security

The toolkit has **no self-installer and no self-update downloader by design**: version
checks only *notify*; installing a new toolkit version is always a manual download from the
official Releases page followed by verification (`verify.ps1`). There is no
user-configurable update URL anywhere in the program or its config.

Updating **dsh itself** (`update` / menu 8) follows a guarded chain:

1. Source is the official npm registry by default (`registry.npmjs.org`); the China mirror
   (`registry.npmmirror.com`) is used only when you explicitly pick it per install.
2. Version strings returned by npm pass a strict whitelist (numeric core + optional
   prerelease); anything else is rejected (command-injection protection).
3. A pre-update backup is created automatically and kept per the retention policy.
4. After install, the resulting version is re-verified; on failure the previous state is
   rolled back and re-checked.
5. High-risk operations (uninstall/wipe, restore, update dsh) first pass a **self-integrity
   gate**: when a `hashes.txt` ships beside the executable and the executable's SHA-256 does
   not match the manifest entry, the operation is refused with an explanation (tamper
   protection). Development builds without a manifest are not blocked. Boundary: this proves
   only that the exe matches the manifest shipped beside it — it is not proof of publisher
   identity (see
   [What the built-in integrity checks prove](#what-the-built-in-integrity-checks-prove-and-do-not-prove)).

## Runtime safety controls

- **Stop guard + TOCTOU re-verification** — `stop` only kills a :3080 listener whose command
  line verifies as dsh, and re-verifies the listener identity immediately before the kill;
  any pid reuse or listener swap inside the check-then-kill window results in `STOP_FAIL`
  (refusal), never a foreign-process kill.
- **Reparse-point handling** — backup and restore never follow symlinks / junctions /
  reparse points; such entries are skipped and recorded in `logs\launcher.log` (audit).
- **No silent half-states** — destructive flows (wipe, restore, update) either complete,
  refuse with a reason, or roll back; see the sections above for each gate.
- **Read-only status & integrity reporting** — `status --detail` (the three-state marker line
  plus `STATUS_PID` / `STATUS_START` / `STATUS_UPTIME`) writes nothing and changes no state,
  and neither does any integrity check: the doctor `Integrity` category, the GUI's startup
  consistency check against the bundled `hashes.txt`, and the About-page "Verify This
  Install" button only inspect, compare and print.
- **TLS 1.2 is enabled explicitly** for the program's HTTPS requests; .NET Framework's default
  `SecurityProtocol` omits it, which made every GitHub HTTPS request (update check, integrity
  check) fail with "could not create SSL/TLS secure channel" before v2.7.0.

## Reporting a Vulnerability

If you discover a security issue — especially anything involving:

- data deletion / wipe behavior,
- backup / restore / import path handling,
- or exposure of credentials stored inside the dsh data directory,

please **report it privately** instead of opening a public issue:

- Use GitHub's private report flow: https://github.com/sakanamaru/dsh-minato/security/advisories/new
- Or contact the maintainer: https://github.com/sakanamaru

Please include:

1. A short description of the issue.
2. The release tag / commit you tested.
3. Steps to reproduce (paths, OS version, what ran).
4. Any relevant output or proof-of-concept.

## Scope

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| This repository's latest release tag | **DeepSeek Harness itself** (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/dsh) |
| The toolkit's own source (`dsh_v2.cs`) and CI pipeline | Node.js / npm / third-party packages |
| Backup / restore / wipe data handling | |

## Permission boundary (what the program may touch)

The toolkit **never asks for administrator rights** (no UAC elevation, no manifest
`requireAdministrator`). It runs as the current standard user and:

| Does | Does NOT |
|---|---|
| Read/write a small state area next to the exe (`launcher.config`, `backups\`, `logs\`) | Write registry `Run` keys, install Windows services, or touch system files |
| Read your dsh data directory when backing up / restoring / wiping (see below) | Access your browser, clipboard, credential store, or other users' data |
| Run `npm install` (with your approval) to install/update dsh | Exfiltrate anything: the program makes no outbound calls beyond the endpoints listed below |

If you see it request administrator elevation or attempt writes outside these areas,
that is a bug — please report it.

## Network endpoints (complete list)

The toolkit only ever connects to these hosts. **Any new endpoint requires a changelog
entry in the release notes** — if you see a connection elsewhere, report it:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `registry.npmjs.org` | Installing / updating dsh (default official npm registry) |
| `registry.npmmirror.com` | Optional China mirror for installs (`L` picker) |
| `api.github.com` / `github.com` | Version check (new release lookup); opening the GitHub page when you press `G`; downloading the official `hashes.txt` when you click "Verify This Install" (GUI About page) |
| `127.0.0.1:3080` | Your local dsh web service (health probe, status monitoring) |

There is **no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting**, and no connection except
the ones above and what the npm client itself does for installs. Every HTTPS request the
program makes explicitly enables **TLS 1.2**.

## Data-safety notes

- The toolkit **never deletes your dsh data without explicit interaction**: wipe requires a
  two-step confirmation (today's date + `yes`), the dsh web service must be stopped, and an
  automatic pre-backup is made before wiping, restoring or importing.
- `stop` refuses to kill a process that is not confirmed to be dsh (a foreign program
  holding `127.0.0.1:3080` is never killed — the command fails with an explanation).
- Manual backups (no suffix) are kept forever; only auto/protection backups
  (`-auto`, `-pre-*`) are cleaned by the retention policy.
- Backups are plain files/directories — keep them somewhere you trust.
- This is an unofficial project and is **not affiliated with DeepSeek**.
- `selftest` CLI (or GUI 体检 report) is strictly read-only: it only inspects and prints.

## Verifiability

Every release is built from source by GitHub Actions (see
[build-release.yml](.github/workflows/build-release.yml)); the source == artifact claim
can be checked by building `dsh_v2.cs` yourself with `csc` (see
[Build from Source](README.md)).

- **`hashes.txt`** in each release lists SHA-256 of every artifact; it is generated by CI
  from the same files it built.
- **GPG signature**: `hashes.txt.asc` is a detached signature by the maintainer:
  - Public key: [`keys/sakanamaru-gpg.asc`](keys/sakanamaru-gpg.asc)
  - Fingerprint: `A2F67D170B5BE4845612642C240979232B4E4CE4`
  - Verify with `gpg --verify hashes.txt.asc hashes.txt` (import the key first).
- **`verify.ps1`** automates the release verification (download → SHA-256 → GPG →
  Release / Tag / Commit chain):

  ```powershell
  powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File verify.ps1 -OutDir D:\verify
  ```

  Run it before using a download. It is read-only and installs nothing.

  What `verify.ps1` covers: SHA-256 against the CI-generated manifest, the GPG signature
  (maintainer fingerprint pinned inside the script, checked with a temporary isolated
  keyring), and the Release / Tag / Commit chain. What it does **not** cover: the GitHub
  artifact attestation — verify that separately with `gh attestation verify`; the two checks
  are independent, and neither replaces the other.

### What the built-in integrity checks prove and do not prove

The program also carries its own checks: the About-page **"Verify This Install"** button, the
startup / first-run consistency check against the bundled `hashes.txt` (local only, no
network), and the doctor `Integrity` category. Be precise about their reach:

- They answer **one narrow question**: does this file match the `hashes.txt` that sits next
  to it? A match proves **consistency with the bundled manifest, and nothing more**.
- They do **not** prove publisher identity. An attacker who replaces **both** the executable
  **and** the adjacent `hashes.txt` would pass every one of them.
- Identity and provenance come only from the **GPG-signed `hashes.txt`** (`hashes.txt.asc`,
  checked by `verify.ps1` or `gpg --verify hashes.txt.asc hashes.txt`) and, independently,
  the **GitHub artifact attestation**.
- "Verify This Install" downloads the *official* manifest over HTTPS, and that is still a
  hash-consistency comparison, **not** signature verification.
- All of these checks are **read-only** — they inspect, compare and print, and write nothing.
  So is `status --detail` (the three-state marker line plus `STATUS_PID` / `STATUS_START` /
  `STATUS_UPTIME`), which exists only to feed the GUI status bar.

The program's HTTPS requests explicitly enable **TLS 1.2** (see
[Runtime safety controls](#runtime-safety-controls)) — without that, .NET Framework's default
`SecurityProtocol` made every GitHub request fail, so both the update check and the remote
manifest comparison were impossible.

Note on reproducibility: the project targets the classic .NET Framework `csc.exe`
(no `/deterministic`); binaries differ byte-wise between builds (module MVID), so
byte-identical reproduction is **not** promised — functional equivalence is verified by
the CI test suite (unit + integration) that runs on every push.
